t.title: Pruebas a lo largo del ciclo de vida del desarrollo de software
Gestión de las Actividades de Prueba

t.e: Evaluating work products is one of the typical objectives (1.1.1). Proving the absence of defects is impossible (principle 1), locating and eliminating the cause is debugging, and exhaustive testing is impossible (principle 2).
Providing information to stakeholders to enable informed decision-making (e.g., the release decision) is a typical objective of testing.
The syllabus states that objectives vary depending on the context: work product under test, test level, risks, life cycle, and business factors (corporate structure, competition, time to market).
Verifying compliance with contractual, legal, and regulatory requirements appears literally among the typical objectives of testing.
Checking that the system meets user expectations in its environment is validation. Verifying specified requirements is verification; both are distinct objectives.
Fixing defects is debugging, an activity that is not testing. The other three options are indeed typical objectives of testing.
Debugging reproduces the failure, diagnoses (finds the defect) and fixes it. Executing, re-executing (confirmation testing) and designing tests are testing.
According to 1.1.2, the typical debugging process is: reproducing the failure, diagnosing (finding the defect) and fixing the defect.
When static testing finds a defect, debugging consists only of removing it: there is no need to reproduce or diagnose, because static testing finds defects directly and does not cause failures.
The syllabus indicates that, preferably, confirmation testing is performed by the same person who performed the initial testing.
Testing and debugging are separate activities: testing causes failures (dynamic) or finds defects (static); debugging seeks causes, analyzes them and removes them.
After confirmation, regression checks that the fix has not caused failures in other parts of the test object.

Testers indirectly represent users, as including a representative group of users is usually expensive and unfeasible. Testing does not eliminate defects (that is debugging) nor does it guarantee the absence of defects.
Testing detects defects cost-effectively; they are then removed through debugging, which is not a testing activity. Therefore, it contributes to quality indirectly.

Testing directly evaluates the quality of the test object in various phases, and these measures support decisions such as phase transition or release. Additionally, any stakeholder can use testing skills.
The syllabus mentions that testing may be mandatory due to contractual, legal, or regulatory requirements.
As quality control, testing helps achieve agreed objectives within scope, time, quality, and budget constraints. Its contribution is not limited to the testing team.
The syllabus explains that the alternative (including representative users) is usually not possible due to high costs and the lack of suitable available users.
Testing: product-oriented, corrective, a form of quality control. QA: process-oriented, preventive, everyone's responsibility in the project.
The syllabus states that QA applies to development and testing processes and is everyone's responsibility in the project.
In testing, results are used to correct defects; in QA, they provide feedback on the performance of development and testing processes.
The syllabus cites formal methods (model checking and correctness proofs), simulation, and prototyping as other forms of quality control.
QA is based on the premise that a good process followed correctly produces a good product; therefore, it focuses on implementing and improving processes.
According to 1.2.2, testing is a primary form of quality control. QA is preventive, process-oriented, and applies to both development and testing.

Error (mistake) → defect → failure. The misunderstanding is the error, the incorrect calculation in the code is the defect, and the observed incorrect total is the failure. Time pressure would be a possible root cause.

The syllabus indicates that some defects always cause failures when executed, others only under specific circumstances, and others never. Additionally, defects in early products often cause defects in later products.
Failures can also be caused by environmental conditions, such as radiation or electromagnetic fields that cause defects in the firmware.
The root cause is the fundamental reason for a problem (e.g., the situation leading to an error). It is identified through root cause analysis, and addressing it helps prevent similar defects.
Lack of training is a fundamental reason leading to human errors: a root cause. Correcting it can prevent similar defects or reduce their frequency.
Defects can be in documentation (a requirements specification, a test script), in source code, or in supporting work products such as a build file.
"Tests wear out": Repeating the same tests makes them less effective at finding new defects; they need to be modified or new tests created.
The fallacy of the absence of defects: verifying all requirements and correcting all defects does not guarantee that the system satisfies users. In addition to verification, validation is required.

"Testing shows the presence, not the absence of defects": even if no defects are found, testing cannot demonstrate that the test object is correct; it only reduces the probability that defects remain.
Since testing everything is not feasible except in trivial cases, the syllabus recommends techniques, prioritization, and risk-based testing to focus effort.
Defect clustering: a small number of components contain the majority of defects (Pareto principle). Expected and observed clusters feed into risk-based testing.
There is no universal testing approach: testing is done differently in different contexts.
Defects removed early do not cause derived defects and reduce the cost of quality; therefore, it is advisable to start early with static and dynamic testing.
The syllabus indicates that, in some cases, repeating the same tests is beneficial, for example in automated regression testing.
Principle 4 (defects cluster) explicitly mentions that clusters of defects, both expected and observed, are an important input for risk-based testing.
10^12 combinations cannot be tested: exhaustive testing is impossible except in trivial cases. Techniques and prioritization must be used.
Analysis answers "what to test": the test basis is analyzed and test conditions are defined and prioritized. Design answers "how to test".

Closure occurs at milestones (release, end of iteration...): useful testware is archived, lessons learned are collected, the environment is left in an agreed state, and the completion report is written.
Design ("how to test") converts conditions into test cases and other testware (e.g., test charters), identifies coverage items, and defines data and environment requirements.

In implementation, the necessary testware for execution (data) is created or acquired, procedures are organized into suites, scripts are created, the execution schedule is prepared, and the environment is built and verified.
Monitoring compares actual progress with the plan; control takes the necessary actions to meet test objectives.
The syllabus indicates that, although they may seem to follow a logical sequence, activities are usually performed iteratively or in parallel and must be adapted to the system and the project.
Context factors: stakeholders, team members, business domain, technical factors, project constraints, organizational factors, the lifecycle, and tools.
Context factors affect the strategy, techniques, degree of automation, required coverage, level of detail of testware, and reporting.
The syllabus lists "Team members (skills, knowledge, level of experience, availability, training needs)" as a context-specific factor.
Scope, time, budget, and resources are project constraints.
Testing is not done in isolation: it is part of the organization's development processes and is funded by stakeholders to meet their business needs.
Software type, product architecture, and technology used are technical factors.
Implementation products: procedures, manual and automated scripts, suites, data, execution schedule, and environment elements (stubs, drivers, simulators, service virtualization).
Analysis produces test conditions (prioritized), such as acceptance criteria, and defect reports from the test basis. Test charters are from design; logs are from execution.
The syllabus cites them as examples of test environment items, which are products of test implementation.
Execution produces test logs and defect reports.
All of them are products of test design ("how to test").
Planning products: test plan, schedule, risk register, and entry and exit criteria. Progress reports are from test monitoring and control.
Traceability allows evaluating coverage, determining the impact of changes, facilitates audits, and helps meet IT governance criteria.
The syllabus gives this example: tracing results to risks allows evaluating the residual risk of the test object.
Tracing test cases to requirements allows verifying that requirements are covered.
Including the status of test basis items makes reports more understandable and helps communicate technical aspects to stakeholders.
Accurate traceability supports coverage assessment; measurable coverage criteria can function as KPIs indicating the extent to which objectives are met.
Good traceability facilitates audits, helps meet IT governance criteria, and provides information on product quality, process capability, and project progress.
The test management role assumes overall responsibility for the process and focuses on planning, monitoring, control, and closure.
The testing role assumes responsibility for the engineering (technical) aspect of testing: analysis, design, implementation, and execution.
The syllabus indicates that different people can assume the roles at different times, and that the same person can have both at the same time.
In agile, part of the test management tasks are assumed by the team; those that span multiple teams or the entire organization can be performed by test managers external to the team.
The syllabus gives as examples of who can perform the management role: a team leader, a test manager, or a development lead.
Designing test cases is an engineering task (testing role). Planning, controlling, and closing correspond to the management role.
Testers often bring bad news, and communicating results can be perceived as criticism. Confirmation bias makes it hard to accept contrary information; defects must be communicated constructively.
The syllabus associates technical knowledge with efficiency (e.g., using appropriate tools). Testing knowledge, analytical thinking, and creativity increase effectiveness.
Domain knowledge enables understanding end users and business stakeholders and communicating with them.
According to 1.5.1, being thorough, careful, curious, methodical, and attentive to detail helps in finding defects, especially those that are difficult to detect.
To improve the perception of testing as a destructive activity, information about defects and failures must be communicated constructively.
The syllabus mentions confirmation bias: it can make it difficult to accept information that contradicts what one believes.
In the whole-team approach, anyone with the necessary knowledge can perform any task, and everyone is responsible for quality.
The syllabus indicates that the whole-team approach originates from Extreme Programming.
Advantages: improves team dynamics, communication, and collaboration, and creates synergy by leveraging diverse skills.
Testers help business representatives create appropriate acceptance tests, and agree with developers on the test strategy and automation.
The syllabus states that in contexts such as safety-critical systems, a high level of test independence may be required, so the whole-team approach may not be suitable.
Sharing space (physical or virtual) facilitates communication and interaction.
With developers, testers agree on the test strategy and decide on automation approaches; thus transferring testing knowledge to the team.
Key to the whole-team approach: everyone is responsible for quality.
By working closely with the team, testers transfer testing knowledge and influence product development.
The syllabus states that the whole team approach is supported by the ability to work effectively in a team and contribute to its objectives.
Disadvantages: team isolation, communication problems or adversarial relationship, developers losing a sense of responsibility for quality, and testers seen as a bottleneck.
Author: no independence. Same team colleagues: some. Testers outside the team within the organization: high. Testers external to the organization: very high.
The main advantage is that, due to their different knowledge, perspectives, and biases, independent testers detect different types of defects than developers.
The syllabus recommends several levels of independence: developers in component and component integration, the test team in system and system integration, and business in acceptance.
Independence does not replace familiarity: developers can efficiently find many defects in their own code.
Testers from outside the organization = very high independence.
In sequential models, executable code arrives late, so testers initially participate in requirements reviews, analysis, and design; dynamic testing cannot be performed early.
The choice of lifecycle affects the scope and timing of activities, the detail of documentation, techniques and approach, the degree of automation, and the role of the tester.
Agile development assumes continuous changes; therefore, lightweight documentation and high automation are preferred to facilitate regression.
If each iteration delivers a functional increment, static and dynamic testing can be performed at all levels in each iteration. Frequent delivery requires rapid feedback and extensive regression.
The syllabus indicates that in agile, most manual testing is performed using experience-based techniques, which do not require extensive prior analysis and design.
Delivering increments frequently requires rapid feedback and extensive regression.

Best practices for any lifecycle: each development activity has a corresponding test activity, each level has specific objectives, analysis and design start in the corresponding phase, and testers review drafts as soon as they exist.
Distinct objectives per level allow testing to be complete without unnecessary overlap.
Analysis and design of a level start in the corresponding development phase, in line with the early testing principle.
Reviewing drafts as soon as they exist favors early defect detection and shift left.
Having a test activity for each development activity ensures that all development is subject to quality control.
The syllabus explicitly links this best practice with the early testing principle.
Requiring dynamic testing before reviews goes against shift left. The other three options are good practices from the syllabus.
The syllabus states that this practice allows defects to be detected earlier and supports shift left.
The good practices of 2.1.2 are independent of the chosen lifecycle model.
Having specific objectives for each level allows for completeness while avoiding redundancies.
TDD drives coding through test cases: test → code → refactoring. Given/When/Then is BDD; deriving tests from acceptance criteria is ATDD.
BDD expresses behavior in simple natural language, typically Given/When/Then, and these cases are later translated into executable tests.
ATDD derives tests from acceptance criteria during system design, and they are written before developing that part of the application.
The three define tests before writing code, apply early testing, follow shift left, and support an iterative model.
According to the syllabus, TDD drives coding through test cases, rather than extensive software design.
In BDD, natural language scenarios must be automatically translated into executable tests.
Tests from these approaches can be maintained as automated tests to ensure code quality in future adaptations or refactoring.
The syllabus indicates that these approaches support an iterative development model.
Writing tests before code, making them pass, and refactoring is the TDD cycle.
In ATDD, tests are written before developing the part of the application that must satisfy them.
Benefits: rapid feedback, CI that promotes shift left, stable environments through automation, greater visibility of non-functional aspects, less repetitive manual testing, and lower regression risk.
Risks: defining and setting up the pipeline is required, introducing and maintaining CI/CD tools, and automation demands resources and can be difficult to maintain.
CI encourages developers to submit quality code accompanied by component tests and static analysis, which shifts testing left.
Although DevOps involves extensive automated testing, manual testing is still needed, especially from the user perspective.
The syllabus attributes the reduction of regression risk to the scale and breadth of automated regression testing.
DevOps requires a cultural change that unites development (including testing) and operations, valuing their roles equally.

Shift left practices: reviewing specifications from the tester's perspective, writing tests before code, using CI/CD, static analysis before dynamic testing, and non-functional testing starting at the component level.
Shift left proposes testing earlier, but does not imply neglecting later testing. It may involve more training, effort, or cost initially in exchange for savings later.
Non-functional testing is often done late, with the complete system; starting it at the component level, when possible, is a form of shift left.
The syllabus indicates that for shift left to be effective, stakeholders must be convinced and committed to the concept.
Shift left may require early investment (training, effort, costs) that is expected to be recovered with later savings.
The syllabus cites it as a shift left practice, especially if it is part of an automated process.
In a retrospective, what went well and should be maintained, what did not go well and can be improved, and how to incorporate improvements are discussed.
The syllabus states that results must be recorded and normally form part of the completion report.
Benefits: greater effectiveness and efficiency, better testware, team cohesion and learning, better test basis, and better cooperation between development and testing.
Participants include testers and other roles: developers, architects, product owner, business analysts…
Retrospectives are key to continuous improvement, and it is important to follow up on recommended improvements.
One of the cited benefits is to improve the test basis, addressing deficiencies in the scope and quality of requirements.
Component integration testing tests interfaces and interactions between components and depends heavily on the integration strategy (bottom-up, top-down, big-bang).
Acceptance focuses on validating and demonstrating that the system is ready for deployment, ideally with the intended users.
System integration testing tests interfaces with other systems and external services, preferably in environments similar to the operational one.
Component testing (unit testing) tests isolated components, usually requires harnesses or frameworks, and is typically performed by developers in their environment.
System testing evaluates the overall behavior of the complete system, including end-to-end tasks and non-functional features, and can be performed by an independent team.
Attributes to distinguish levels: test object, objectives, test basis, defects and failures, and approach and responsibilities.
Acceptance forms: UAT, operational, contractual and regulatory, alpha and beta.
Performance efficiency is a non-functional characteristic: it measures "how well" the system behaves.
Functional testing evaluates "what" the system should do: functional completeness, correctness, and adequacy.
White-box testing is based on structure; its main objective is to cover that structure to an acceptable level.
The four types (functional, non-functional, black-box, and white-box) can be applied at all levels, with different focus.
Non-functional characteristics in the syllabus: performance efficiency, compatibility, usability (ability to interact), reliability, security, maintainability, portability (flexibility), and safety.
The syllabus warns that discovering non-functional defects late can seriously endanger the project; therefore, it is sometimes advisable to start early.
Black-box testing is based on specifications and derives tests from documentation unrelated to the internal structure.
Confirmation checks that the original defect has been fixed; regression checks that the change has not had adverse consequences in other parts.
The syllabus allows, with little time or money, to limit confirmation to reproducing the failure steps and checking that it no longer occurs.
It is advisable to perform an impact analysis first, which shows which parts of the software could be affected.
Regression suites are executed many times and grow with each iteration, so they are ideal for automation, starting early.
Adverse consequences can affect the same component, other components in the system, or even connected systems, as well as the environment.
The syllabus indicates that they are needed at all levels where defects are fixed or changes are made.
Triggers: modifications (enhancements, fixes, hot fixes), updates or migrations of the operating environment, and system retirement.
When retiring a system, it may be necessary to test data archiving and restoration and recovery procedures during the archive period.
The scope depends on the risk of the change, the size of the existing system, and the size of the change.
Migrations may require testing of the new environment, the changed software, and data conversion.
Prior impact analysis helps decide whether to make the change based on its possible consequences on other areas of the system.
Maintenance testing evaluates the success of the change and checks for possible regressions in the unmodified parts, which usually constitute the majority of the system.
Almost any work product can be examined with static testing: specifications, code, test plans and test cases, backlog, test charters, project documentation, contracts, and models.
Products that are difficult for people to interpret and should not be analyzed with tools (e.g., third-party executable code for legal reasons) are not suitable.
For a review, it is sufficient that the product can be read and understood; for static analysis, it requires a checkable structure (models, code, or text with formal syntax).
Any work product that can be read and understood can be the object of a review.
The syllabus cites spell checkers and readability tools as examples of static analysis tools.
Testers, business, and developers collaborate in example mapping, collaborative story writing, and backlog refinement so that stories meet criteria such as the Definition of Ready.
Static testing detects defects that dynamic testing cannot (unreachable code, design patterns not implemented as expected, defects in non-executable products).
Although reviews cost, the total cost is usually lower because less is spent on fixing defects later.
By being done early, static testing creates a shared understanding and improves communication, which is why it is advisable to involve many stakeholders.
Verifying documented requirements allows stakeholders to check that they describe their actual needs.
Static analysis detects certain code defects more efficiently, without the need for test cases, and is often integrated into CI. It is also used to evaluate maintainability and security.
Static testing can detect defects in the earliest phases, fulfilling the early testing principle.

Typical of static testing: defects in requirements, design, certain code issues (undefined variables, unreachable or duplicated code), deviations from standards, poorly specified interfaces, certain vulnerabilities, and gaps in coverage of the test basis.
Static testing finds defects directly; dynamic testing causes failures, and the defect is determined afterward through analysis.
Static testing measures characteristics that do not depend on executing code (e.g., maintainability); dynamic testing measures those that do (e.g., performance efficiency).
The syllabus cites incorrect interface specifications as defects that are easier and cheaper to find with static testing.
Static testing does not require executing code, so it more easily finds defects in rare or hard-to-reach paths dynamically.
They are complementary practices with similar objectives, but there are types of defects that only one or the other can detect.
Early and frequent feedback communicates potential quality issues early and avoids misunderstandings about requirements.
With low involvement, the product may not meet the stakeholder's vision: costly rework, missed deadlines, blame-seeking, or even project failure.
It improves understanding of what is being built and allows focusing on what delivers the most value and reduces identified risks the most.
It prevents misunderstandings about requirements and ensures that changes are understood and implemented early.
The syllabus lists costly rework, missed deadlines, blame-seeking, and even complete project failure.
Section 3.2.1 deals precisely with the benefits of early and frequent feedback throughout the entire lifecycle.
Activities: planning, review initiation, individual review, communication and analysis, and correction and reporting. In the individual review, each reviewer examines and records anomalies.
In planning, the scope is defined: purpose, product to be reviewed, quality characteristics, focus areas, exit criteria, supporting information, effort, and schedule.
In initiation, it is ensured that everyone has access to the product, understands their role, and receives what is needed.
In communication and analysis, the status, responsible person, and actions for each anomaly are decided; not all are defects. This is usually done in a review meeting.
In correction and reporting, a report is created for each defect to track it, and when exit criteria are met, the product can be accepted; results are reported.
The ISO/IEC 20246 standard defines a generic review process, structured but flexible, which can be adapted.

The moderator ensures the smooth running of the meetings. The scribe records anomalies and decisions; the review leader assumes overall responsibility; the manager decides what to review and provides resources.
The manager decides what is reviewed and provides the resources.
The scribe (recorder) collects anomalies and records review information.
The review leader assumes overall responsibility: decides who participates and organizes when and where.
The author creates and corrects the reviewed work product.
A reviewer can be someone from the project, a subject matter expert, or any other stakeholder.
Inspection is the most formal: it follows the complete generic process, collects metrics, and seeks to find the maximum number of anomalies. The author cannot be the moderator or the scribe.
The walkthrough is led by the author and can have very varied objectives: to evaluate quality, train reviewers, achieve consensus, generate ideas, or detect anomalies.
Technical review is conducted by technically qualified reviewers, led by a moderator, and seeks consensus and decisions on a technical issue, in addition to detecting anomalies.
Informal reviews do not follow a defined process nor require a formally documented output. Their main objective is to detect anomalies.
In inspections, the author cannot act as the review moderator or as the scribe.
Formality depends on the life cycle, process maturity, product criticality and complexity, legal or regulatory requirements, and the need for an audit trail.
The syllabus indicates that the same product can be reviewed using different types, first an informal one and then a more formal one.
Success factors: clear objectives and measurable exit criteria, appropriate review type, small chunks, feedback, time to prepare, management support, culture, training, and meeting facilitation.
The syllabus is explicit: the evaluation of participants must never be an objective.
Management support is a success factor. Additionally, the appropriate review type must be chosen based on the objective and context, not always the most formal one.
Providing feedback from reviews to stakeholders and authors allows them to improve the product and their activities.
Integrating reviews into the organization's culture promotes learning and process improvement.
Proper training of all participants is a success factor, as is defining clear objectives and measurable exit criteria.
Black-box techniques (specification-based) analyze the specified behavior without looking at the internal structure; therefore, their test cases remain valid if the implementation changes.
White-box techniques (structure-based) analyze the internal structure, so they require the design or implementation.
Experience-based techniques leverage the tester's knowledge; their effectiveness depends heavily on their skills and complement black-box and white-box techniques.
Black-box = specification-based; white-box = structure-based.
White-box techniques are also called structure-based.
Techniques support analysis (what to test) and design (how to test): they help define conditions, identify coverage items, and test data.
Analyzing code branches is a white-box technique (branch testing).
Equivalence partitioning applied to specified requirements is a black-box technique.
Anticipating defects from experience (error guessing) is an experience-based technique.
Techniques help to systematically obtain a relatively small but sufficient set of cases.

In statement testing, the coverage items are executable statements.
Statement coverage = exercised statements / total executable statements, in percentage.
100% statement coverage guarantees that every statement is executed, but it does not detect all defects (e.g., data-dependent ones) nor does it guarantee that all branches are exercised.
An IF without an ELSE can be covered with true output by executing all statements, without ever testing the false output.
A single test with a = 11 and b = 6 executes all statements (both conditions are true). Statement coverage does not require testing false outputs.
The syllabus states that with 100% coverage, each statement with a defect is executed, which may cause a failure that demonstrates its presence.
Coverage = 30 / 40 = 75%.
Any set that achieves 100% branch coverage achieves 100% statement coverage, but not vice versa.
A branch is a control transfer between two nodes in the control flow graph; it can be unconditional (linear code) or conditional (result of a decision).
The true and false exits of the two decisions must be traversed. A test with both true and another with both false achieve this: 2 tests.
Conditional branches correspond to the true/false results of an IF, the outputs of a switch/case, or the decision to exit or continue a loop.
Exercising all branches does not guarantee detecting defects that only appear when traversing a specific path.
Branch coverage = exercised branches / total branches, as a percentage.
Both exits of the decision are needed: x > 0 (e.g., 5) and x ≤ 0 (e.g., -5). A single value covers only one branch, and 5, 6, and 7 all traverse the same one.
The strength of white-box testing is that it considers the entire implementation, which is useful even if the specification is vague, obsolete, or incomplete.
If a requirement is not implemented, there is no code to cover, so white-box testing may not detect that omission defect.
White-box techniques are applicable in static testing: dry runs of code, code review of non-executable code, pseudocode, and logic that can be modeled with a control flow graph.
With black-box testing alone, actual code coverage is not measured; white-box testing provides an objective measure and allows for the generation of additional tests.
White-box coverage metrics provide an objective measure and information to create additional tests, which increases confidence in the code.
The syllabus indicates that white-box testing fits in reviews of pseudocode and other high-level logic that can be modeled with a control flow graph.

The syllabus only covers statement and branch testing; it mentions more rigorous techniques (critical environments), higher-level techniques (APIs), and code-agnostic coverage (neural coverage) as out of scope.
Error guessing anticipates errors, defects, and failures based on the tester's knowledge: how the application worked, typical developer errors, and failures in similar applications.
Fault attacks are a way to implement error guessing: a list of possible errors, defects, and failures is created or acquired, and tests are designed to provoke or expose them.
Sources: how the application worked in the past, typical developer errors, and failures in similar applications.
Choosing inputs because they have historically caused failures is error guessing (related to input errors).
The syllabus lists: input, output, logic, calculation, interfaces, and data.
Lists can be based on experience, defect and failure data, or common knowledge of why software fails.
The syllabus gives "missing cases, wrong operator" as examples of logic errors.
Exploratory testing is useful with sparse or poor specifications, under time pressure, and to complement more formal techniques. It is more effective with experienced testers.
In exploratory testing, test design, execution, and evaluation are performed simultaneously while learning about the test object.
In the session-based approach, work is done in a timebox guided by a test charter with objectives; this is usually followed by a debriefing.
After the session, there is usually a debriefing with stakeholders interested in the results.
Exploratory testing may incorporate other techniques, such as equivalence partitioning. Coverage items are identified and exercised during the session.
The tester may use test session sheets to document the steps and findings.
The syllabus indicates that exploratory testing is more effective with experienced testers, with domain knowledge and with analytical skills, curiosity and creativity.
The syllabus states that checklists should not include items that can be checked automatically, nor other more suitable ones such as entry or exit criteria, nor too general ones.
Some inputs lose effectiveness because developers learn to avoid those errors, and others must be added for new serious defects, taking care that the list does not become too long.
Without detailed cases, checklists provide guidelines and some consistency. If they are high-level there will be variability: more potential coverage, but less repeatability.
With high-level lists, each tester tests somewhat differently: coverage can be increased, but repeatability is reduced.
List items are usually formulated as questions, each of which can be checked separately and directly.
The syllabus cites the 10 usability heuristics (Nielsen) as an example of a checklist for non-functional testing.
Lists can be based on experience, on what is important to the user, or on understanding why and how the software fails.
Card: the artifact that describes the user story. Conversation: how the software will be used. Confirmation: the acceptance criteria.
Good user stories meet INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, and testable.
Collaboration allows a shared vision of what needs to be delivered from three perspectives: business, development, and testing.
The syllabus indicates that it may mean the story is unclear, does not reflect something valuable, or the stakeholder needs help to test.
Usual format: "As a [role], I want [goal], so that I can [business value]", followed by acceptance criteria.
The syllabus mentions brainstorming and mind maps.
Given/When/Then is the scenario-oriented format (BDD). The rule-oriented format uses checklists or input-output tables.
A checklist with bullet points (or an input-output table) is the rule-oriented format.
They are used to define the scope, achieve consensus, describe positive and negative scenarios, serve as a basis for acceptance, and enable accurate planning and estimation.
The syllabus indicates that acceptance criteria usually result from the Conversation; the criteria themselves are the Confirmation. "Commitment" and "Coverage" are not part of the 3 C's.
Acceptance criteria can be seen as the test conditions that must be exercised.
The syllabus allows a custom format as long as the criteria are well-defined and unambiguous.
In ATDD, positive tests are normally started first, followed by negative tests and finally non-functional tests.
The first step is a specification workshop where the user story and its acceptance criteria are analyzed and written, resolving ambiguities.
ATDD tests are based on the acceptance criteria of the user story and do not go beyond it. This covers AC2; the other options test functionalities outside the user story.
Tests must cover all features of the user story without going beyond it, and there should not be two tests that describe the same feature.
Typical order: positive cases → negative cases → non-functional characteristics (e.g., performance efficiency, usability).
In ATDD test design, techniques such as BVA can be applied: the boundary (200) should be accepted and the next value (201) rejected with the message.
Cases are created from different perspectives (customer, developer, tester); after the workshop, the entire team or the tester can write them.
They must be understandable to stakeholders: sentences in natural language with preconditions, inputs, and postconditions.
That way the acceptance tests become executable requirements.
One case per characteristic is needed: accepted format, unsupported format, and excessive size. Repeating the same positive case adds no value, and the last option contradicts the criteria.
Typical content: context, assumptions and constraints, stakeholders, communication, risk register, test approach, budget and schedule.
A plan documents means and schedule, helps to meet criteria, serves for communication, and demonstrates adherence to the test policy and strategy (or explains deviations).
Preparing the plan forces thinking about future challenges (risks, schedule, people, tools, costs, effort).
The syllabus places hiring and training needs within the stakeholders section of the plan.
The ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 standard covers test documentation, including the plan.
One of the purposes of the plan is to demonstrate adherence to the test policy and strategy or to explain deviations.

In release planning, testers participate in writing user stories and verifiable acceptance criteria, in project and quality risk analysis, estimate effort, determine the approach, and plan the release testing.

In iteration planning, testers analyze the risks of user stories in detail, determine their testability, break them down into tasks (primarily testing tasks), estimate, and refine functional and non-functional aspects.
Iteration planning looks at the end of an iteration and works with the iteration backlog; release planning looks at the release and the product backlog.
Release planning defines and redefines the product backlog, can split large user stories, and is the basis for the approach and test plan for all iterations.
Testers break down user stories into tasks (primarily testing tasks) and estimate the effort for all of them.
The syllabus indicates that in iterative life cycles, two types of planning typically occur: release planning and iteration planning.
Output: completeness measures (coverage, unresolved defects, density, failed tests) and yes/no criteria. Available requirements, ready environment, and passed smoke tests are entry criteria.
Input: availability of resources and testware, and initial quality level of the test object (e.g., passed smoke tests).
Exit criteria are often called Definition of Done; entry criteria for a user story are called Definition of Ready.
Running out of time or budget can be acceptable if stakeholders accept the risk of exiting without further testing.
The syllabus warns that without meeting entry criteria, the activity will likely be more difficult, longer, more expensive, and riskier.
Entry and exit criteria must be defined for each level and differ according to objectives.

The higher the layer: the less granularity, less isolation, and more execution time. At the bottom, many tests are needed; at the top, few.
The original model (Cohn 2009) defines unit, service, and UI tests. Another popular model uses unit, integration, and end-to-end.
Higher up: lower granularity, lower isolation (more dependency on other items), and more execution time.
The pyramid supports automation and effort allocation by showing that different objectives are covered with different levels of automation.
The number and name of the layers may vary; other test levels may also be used.
Tests at the base are small, isolated, and fast, and check a small piece, so many are needed.

Q1: technical, support the team (component and component integration testing). Q2: business, support the team (functional, examples, user stories, UX prototypes, API, simulations). Q3: business, critique the product (exploratory, usability, UAT). Q4: technical, critique the product (smoke and non-functional except usability).
Q1 = technology-oriented and supporting the team: component and component integration testing, automated and in CI.
Q3 groups user-oriented tests that critique the product, often manual: exploratory, usability, and UAT.
Q2 checks acceptance criteria and can be manual or automated.
The quadrants combine two axes: business or technology-oriented, and supporting the team or critiquing the product.
The quadrants were defined by Brian Marick (Marick 2003, Crispin 2008). The test pyramid is by Cohn.
Usability is in Q3; Q4 contains non-functional aspects except usability.
The model helps visualize that all appropriate test types and levels are included, and that some types are more relevant at certain levels.
Tests in Q2 (business, team support) verify acceptance criteria.
"Support the team" = guide development; "critique the product" = measure behavior against expectations.
Risk level combines the probability of occurrence with the impact (damage) if it occurs.
Risk probability is between 0 and 1 (exclusive); impact is the damage or consequences.
A risk is a potential event, danger, threat, or situation whose occurrence causes an adverse effect.
The risk level is a measure: the higher, the more important its treatment.
The syllabus defines the impact of risk (harm) as the consequences of its occurrence.
With the same probability, the risk with greater impact has a higher risk level.
Project risks affect management and control: organizational, personnel, technical, and supplier risks. The others are product risks.
Product risks are linked to quality characteristics: functionality, calculations, runtime errors, architecture, algorithms, response time, user experience, security.
Uncontrolled scope creep and poor tool support are project risks of a technical nature.
Project risks can affect the schedule, budget, or scope, and therefore the ability to meet objectives.
Consequences of product risks: user dissatisfaction, loss of revenue or reputation, harm to third parties, high maintenance costs, criminal penalties, and even physical harm.
Project risks of the 'people' type include insufficient skills, conflicts, communication problems, and lack of staff.
Risk analysis = identification + assessment. Risk control = mitigation + monitoring.
The results determine scope, levels and types, techniques and coverage, effort, prioritization, and other activities besides testing.
Quantitative: level = probability × impact. Qualitative: a risk matrix is used.
The syllabus mentions brainstorming, workshops, interviews, and cause-effect diagrams.
The objective is to focus test effort to minimize the residual product risk, ideally starting early in the lifecycle.
Categorization helps assign mitigation actions, because risks of the same category are usually mitigated in a similar way.

Test mitigation: appropriate testers, appropriate level of independence, reviews and static analysis, appropriate techniques and coverage, appropriate test types, and dynamic testing (including regression).
Answer options: test mitigation, acceptance, transfer, or contingency plan. An insurance policy transfers the risk.
Monitoring checks the effectiveness of mitigation, improves assessment, and identifies emerging risks.
Product risk control = mitigation + monitoring.
Applying the appropriate level of independence is one of the test-based mitigation actions.
Deciding not to act on a risk is risk acceptance.
Defect metrics: number and priority of defects found/fixed, density, detection percentage. Mean time to failure is a product quality metric.
The syllabus classifies requirements coverage and code coverage as coverage metrics.
Product quality metrics: availability, response time, mean time to failure.
The residual risk level is a risk metric.
Test progress metrics: implementation progress of test cases, environment preparation, executed/not executed test cases, passed/failed, execution time.
Metrics show progress against schedule and budget, current quality and test effectiveness, and support control and closure.
The progress report is periodic and supports control. The final assessment, lessons learned, and unmitigated risks are included in the completion report.
Completion report: summary, assessment against the plan, deviations, impediments, metrics, unmitigated risks, uncorrected defects, and lessons learned.
Prepared at closure, when a project, test level, or test type ends, ideally after meeting the exit criteria.
Different audiences need different information: progress reports within the team are usually frequent and informal; the completion report follows a template and is produced once.
Progress reports support ongoing control and should allow changes to the schedule, resources, or plan when necessary.
Standard 29119-3 refers to progress reports as test status reports.
Options: verbal communication, dashboards, electronic channels (email, chat), online documentation, and formal reports. These can be combined.
In distributed teams, more formal communication may be more appropriate due to distance or time zone differences.
Each stakeholder is interested in different information, so communication must be adapted.
The syllabus indicates that, in self-organizing teams, the team itself decides the best medium.
Email and chat are electronic communication channels.
Several options can be combined; the best one depends on test management, the organization's strategy, regulations, or the team itself.
In testing, configuration management is a discipline to identify, control, and track work products as configuration items.
Once approved for testing, the item becomes a baseline and can only be changed through formal change control.
Configuration management records changes by creating a new baseline and allows reverting to a previous one to reproduce results.
For complex items, it records their components, their relationships, and their versions.
It ensures unique identification, version control, change tracking, and relationships between items (traceability), and that testware unambiguously references documentation and software.
CI, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment are typically implemented in an automated DevOps pipeline, which usually includes automated configuration management.
The syllabus lists these testware as potential configuration items.
The syllabus defines test items as individual parts of the test object.
Configuration management ensures that the identified documentation and software are unambiguously referenced in the testware.
Configuration management records versions and relationships of items (build, data, environment), enabling the reproduction of previous results.

A report contains identifier, title, date, organization and author, object and environment, context, description for reproduction, expected and actual result, severity, priority, status, and references. Blaming others is of no value.
To reproduce and resolve, the expected result, the data used (username, password), and the version of the object and environment are needed. The other options do not help with resolution.
Severity measures the impact on stakeholders or requirements (here low); priority, the urgency of correction (here high due to the demo).
The impact (data corruption) is high, but the urgency is low because the functionality will not be published soon.
Objectives: provide sufficient information to resolve, allow tracking of product quality, and provide ideas for process improvement.

Reported anomalies may turn out not to be defects (e.g., a false positive). Rejecting is the appropriate status. Examples of status: open, deferred, duplicate, waiting to be fixed, awaiting confirmation testing, re-opened, closed, rejected.
The context includes the executed test case, the activity, the lifecycle phase, and other relevant information (technical, checklist, data).
The title should briefly summarize the anomaly. The other options are vague or accusatory.
After the fix is delivered, the report remains pending confirmation testing before being closed.
A duplicate report is marked as such and references the existing one; "duplicate" is one of the statuses cited in the syllabus.

Syllabus categories: test management, static testing, design and implementation, execution and coverage, non-functional testing, DevOps, collaboration, deployment scalability and standardization, and any other tool that helps.
Execution and coverage tools facilitate automated execution and coverage measurement.
Test management tools facilitate lifecycle management, requirements, tests, defects, and configuration.
Non-functional testing tools enable tests that are difficult or impossible to perform manually.
DevOps tools support the delivery pipeline, flow tracking, automated builds, and CI/CD.
Design and implementation tools facilitate the generation of test cases, test data, and test procedures.
Static testing tools support reviews and static analysis.
The syllabus explicitly states that any tool that helps with testing (e.g., a spreadsheet) is a test tool in that context.
Collaboration tools make communication easier.
Containers for standardizing and scaling environment deployments belong to this category.

Benefits: saving manual repetitive work, preventing human errors (consistency and repeatability), more objective evaluation, easier access to information, faster execution, and more time to design better tests.

Risks: unrealistic expectations, inaccurate estimates, using the tool when manual testing is more appropriate, over-reliance on the tool, vendor dependency, abandoned open source, incompatibility with the platform, or non-compliance with regulations.
Underestimating the time, cost, and effort to introduce the tool and maintain the scripts is a typical risk.
A more objective assessment and measures that are too complex to perform manually are a benefit of automation.

Using a tool when manual testing is more appropriate appears among the risks of automation.

t.sum: Testing is a set of activities to discover defects and assess the quality of work products (test objects). It is not just execution: it also includes static activities, planning, management… and combines verification (does it meet specifications?) with validation (does it cover real needs?). Typical objectives: assess work products, provoke failures and find defects, ensure coverage, reduce risk, verify requirements and legal compliance, report to stakeholders to decide, generate confidence, and validate. Objectives change depending on the context.

Testing and debugging are distinct activities. Dynamic testing causes failures; static testing finds defects directly. Debugging seeks the cause (the defect), analyzes it, and eliminates it: reproduce → diagnose → correct. This is followed by confirmation testing (preferably performed by the person who conducted the initial testing) and regression testing. If the defect was found by static testing, it is sufficient to eliminate it.

Testing is a cost-effective way to detect defects, which are then eliminated through debugging: it contributes to quality indirectly. It measures quality at each phase and supports decisions (such as release), indirectly represents users (involving them directly is usually expensive), and may be mandatory by contract, law, or regulation.

Testing ≠ QA. Testing is product-oriented and corrective: it is a form of quality control, as are formal methods, simulation, or prototyping. QA is process-oriented and preventive (a good process yields a good product), and is everyone's responsibility. Test results serve testing to correct defects and serve QA as feedback on processes.

A person commits an error (mistake) that introduces a defect (bug, fault) into a work product; if the defect is executed, it may produce a failure. Not every defect always produces a failure, and some failures are due to the environment (radiation, electromagnetic fields). The root cause is the fundamental reason for the problem; addressing it prevents similar defects.

1) Testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence. 2) Exhaustive testing is impossible: techniques, prioritization, and risks must be used. 3) Testing early saves time and money. 4) Defects cluster (Pareto), which feeds risk-based testing. 5) Tests wear out: repeating them makes them ineffective at finding new defects, except in automated regression. 6) Testing is context-dependent. 7) Fallacy of absence of defects: verification is not enough; validation is also required.

Planning (objectives and approach) · Monitoring and control (compare with the plan and correct) · Analysis ("what to test": prioritized conditions derived from the test basis) · Design ("how to test": cases, test charters, coverage items, data and environment requirements) · Implementation (procedures, scripts, suites, data, execution schedule, ready environment) · Execution (execute, compare, record, analyze anomalies) · Closure (archive testware, completion report, lessons learned). These are usually performed iteratively or in parallel.

The way of testing depends on the context: stakeholders, team, business domain (criticality, risks, regulations), technical factors, project constraints (scope, time, budget), organization, lifecycle, and tools. This affects the strategy, techniques, automation, coverage, detail of testware, and reporting.

Each activity produces testware. Planning: plan, schedule, risk register, entry and exit criteria. Monitoring and control: progress reports, control directives. Analysis: prioritized conditions (e.g., acceptance criteria) and defect reports from the test basis. Design: cases, test charters, coverage items, data and environment requirements. Implementation: procedures, scripts, suites, data, execution schedule, stubs, drivers, simulators. Execution: logs and defect reports. Closure: completion report, lessons learned, change requests.

Maintaining traceability between test basis, testware, results, and defects allows evaluating coverage (requirements covered, residual risk), analyzing the impact of changes, facilitating audits and IT governance, and producing understandable reports that show the status of each element of the test basis.

There are two main roles. Test management: responsible for the process and the team; focuses on planning, monitoring, control, and closure. Testing: responsible for the technical aspect; focuses on analysis, design, implementation, and execution. One person can have both roles; in agile, part of the management is assumed by the team.

Key skills: testing knowledge (effectiveness), thoroughness and curiosity (finding difficult defects), communication and active listening, analytical and critical thinking and creativity, technical knowledge (efficiency) and domain knowledge (speaking with users). Since the tester often delivers bad news, they must communicate defects constructively, taking into account confirmation bias.

It comes from Extreme Programming: anyone with the necessary skill can perform any task, and everyone is responsible for quality. They share the space (physical or virtual). Advantages: better dynamics, communication, and collaboration, and synergy. Testers help the business with acceptance testing and agree with development on strategy and automation. It may not fit critical systems that require high independence.

Levels: author (none), team peers (some), testers from outside the team but within the organization (high), external testers (very high). It is usually ideal to combine several levels. Advantages: they detect other types of defects and question assumptions. Disadvantages: isolation, communication issues, developers lose responsibility for quality, and testers are seen as a bottleneck.

The lifecycle conditions the scope and timing of testing, the detail of documentation, the techniques, automation, and the tester's role. Sequential: at the beginning, reviews, analysis, and design; dynamic testing comes late. Iterative and incremental: static and dynamic testing in each iteration, fast feedback, and extensive regression testing. Agile: lightweight documentation, heavy automation, and manual experience-based testing.

For any lifecycle: 1) each development activity has a corresponding testing activity; 2) each test level has distinct objectives (complete and non-redundant); 3) analysis and design start in the corresponding development phase (early testing); 4) testers review drafts as soon as they exist (shift left).

TDD: tests (usually component-level) before code; test → code → refactoring cycle. ATDD: tests derived from acceptance criteria during system design, before development. BDD: behavior in natural language (Given/When/Then) that is later translated into executable tests. All three apply early testing and shift left, support iterative development, and their tests can be maintained as automated.

DevOps unites development (including testing) and operations through a cultural change, CI/CD, and an automated pipeline. Benefits: fast feedback, CI drives shift left (component testing and static analysis), stable environments, greater visibility of non-functional aspects, less repetitive manual testing, and lower regression risk. Challenges: setting up and maintaining the pipeline and tools, and the cost of automation. Manual testing from the user perspective is still needed.

Shift left means testing earlier, without neglecting late testing. Practices: reviewing specifications as a tester, writing tests before code, CI/CD with component testing, static analysis before dynamic testing, and non-functional testing starting at the component level. It costs more initially but saves later, and requires stakeholder support.

In retrospectives (at the end of an iteration, release, or project, or when needed), what worked, what to improve, and how to apply improvements are analyzed. The entire team participates, not just testers. Results usually go into the completion report. Benefits: greater effectiveness and efficiency, better testware, team learning and cohesion, better test basis, and improved cooperation between development and testing. Improvement actions must be tracked.

Component (isolated units, with harness or frameworks, by developers) · Component integration (interfaces between components; depends on bottom-up, top-down, or big-bang strategy) · System (global behavior, end-to-end, and non-functional; often by an independent team) · System integration (interfaces with other systems and external services) · Acceptance (validation and readiness for deployment: UAT, operational, contractual, regulatory, alpha, and beta). They are distinguished by test object, objectives, test basis, defects, and responsibilities.

Functional: what the system does (functional completeness, correctness, and adequacy). Non-functional: how well it does it (ISO 25010: performance, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability, safety); it is advisable to start early. Black-box: based on specification. White-box: based on structure, to cover it. All four types are applied at all levels.

Confirmation: verify that the original defect was fixed (re-execute failed tests, add new tests, or, if time is short, reproduce the failure steps). Regression: verify that the change has not caused adverse effects in the same component, in other components, or in connected systems, as well as in the environment. An impact analysis should be performed, and regression is a strong candidate for automation. Both are necessary at all levels where changes occur.

Changes to a production system are tested: the change itself and regression on what did not change. The scope depends on the risk, the size of the system, and the size of the change. Triggers: modifications (enhancements, fixes, hot fixes), environment updates or migrations (including data conversion), and decommissioning (data archiving, restoration, and recovery). Prior impact analysis helps decide whether to make the change.

Almost any product can be examined: requirements, code, test plans and test cases, backlog, test charters, documentation, contracts, and models. To review, it is sufficient that it can be read and understood; for static testing, a verifiable structure (formal syntax) is required. Not suitable, for example, third-party executable code that should not be analyzed for legal reasons.

Detects defects very early (early testing) and even some that dynamic testing does not see: unreachable code, poorly applied design patterns, defects in non-executable products. Creates shared understanding among stakeholders and improves communication. Reviews cost, but reduce project costs, and static testing finds certain code defects more efficiently.

They are complementary. Static testing finds defects directly; dynamic testing causes failures and then the defect is analyzed. Static testing reaches rare code paths, is applied to non-executable products, and measures aspects that do not depend on execution (maintainability); dynamic testing measures what depends on execution (performance). Typical of static testing: requirements and design defects, certain code defects, deviations from standards, poorly specified interfaces, some vulnerabilities, and coverage gaps.

Communicate quality issues early, avoid misunderstandings about requirements, help understand and implement changes early, and focus on what delivers the most value. Without feedback: costly rework, missed deadlines, blame-seeking, and even project failure.

Generic process according to ISO/IEC 20246: Planning (scope, purpose, quality characteristics, exit criteria, effort, deadlines) → Review initiation (ensure everyone has access and understands their role) → Individual review (each reviewer notes anomalies, recommendations, and questions using techniques such as checklists or scenarios) → Communication and analysis (decide status, responsible person, and actions for each anomaly; quality level) → Correction and reporting (defect reports, acceptance upon meeting exit criteria).

Manager: decides what is reviewed and provides resources. Author: creates and corrects the product. Moderator (facilitator): leads meetings with mediation, time management, and a safe environment. Recorder: collects anomalies and records decisions. Reviewer: reviews (any stakeholder). Review leader: overall responsible; decides who participates, when, and where.

Informal: no defined process or formal output; objective is to detect anomalies. Walkthrough: led by the author; varied objectives (evaluate, train, achieve consensus, generate ideas, detect anomalies). Technical review: technical reviewers led by a moderator; seek consensus and technical decisions. Inspection: the most formal; complete process, metrics, objective to find the maximum number of anomalies; the author cannot be the leader or recorder. Formality depends on the lifecycle, criticality, regulations, and audit requirements.

Clear objectives and measurable exit criteria (never evaluate participants), appropriate review type, small chunks, feedback to authors and stakeholders, time to prepare, management support, reviews as part of the culture, training for all participants, and well-facilitated meetings.

Techniques assist in analysis (what) and design (how) to obtain a small but sufficient set of test cases. Black-box (specification-based): independent of implementation, they remain valid if the code changes but the behavior does not. White-box (structure-based): depend on the design, so they can only be created afterwards. Experience-based: depend on the tester's skill and find what the others miss.

example.problem: A field accepts integer grades from 0 to 100: 0–49 fail, 50–69 pass, 70–100 good. Outside 0–100 is rejected. How many minimum values are needed for 100% partition coverage?
steps: Valid partitions: 0–49, 50–69, 70–100 (3).
Invalid partitions: < 0 and > 100 (2).
Total: 5 partitions; one value per partition.
Example set: −5, 20, 60, 85, 120 → 5 values, 100% coverage.
example.title: Solved exercise

t.sum: Divides data into partitions that the system treats equally: one value per partition is sufficient. Partitions do not overlap and cannot be empty, and they can be valid or invalid. Coverage items = partitions (including invalid ones); coverage = exercised partitions / total. With multiple inputs, Each Choice coverage requires exercising each partition of each set at least once, without combining.

example.problem: Valid age 18–65 (integers). Obtain the values for 2-value BVA and those added by 3-value BVA.
steps: Partitions: ≤ 17 (invalid), 18–65 (valid), ≥ 66 (invalid).
Boundary values: 17 | 18 and 65 | 66.
2-value BVA: {17, 18, 65, 66} → 4 coverage items.
3-value BVA: each boundary with its two neighbors; adds values like 19 and 64, which are not boundaries.
Coverage = exercised values / identified coverage items.
example.title: Solved exercise

t.sum: Only applies to ordered partitions. Boundary values are the minimum and maximum of each partition. 2-value BVA: for each boundary, the boundary value and its closest neighbor from the adjacent partition (i.e., all boundary values). 3-value BVA: the boundary and its two neighbors; it is more rigorous. Syllabus example: if "x ≤ 10" was implemented as "x = 10", values 10 and 11 do not detect it, but 9 does.

example.problem: Discount: C1 member, C2 order > 100 €, C3 coupon. How many columns does the full table have and how many tests are needed if C1 and "guest" (C4) cannot both be true?
steps: With 3 conditions: 2^3 = 8 columns.
If we add C4 (guest): 2^4 = 16 columns.
Combinations with C1 = T and C4 = T are infeasible: 2^2 = 4 columns.
Feasible columns: 16 − 4 = 12 → 12 tests for 100% coverage (without merging).
example.title: Solved exercise

t.sum: Useful for logic with combinations of conditions (business rules). Rows are conditions and actions; each column is a rule. Notation: T/F, "–" (irrelevant), "N/A" (infeasible); X = the action occurs. The full table has 2^n columns with n boolean conditions; infeasible combinations are removed and columns may be merged. Coverage items = feasible columns. Helps find gaps and contradictions in requirements.

example.problem: Player: Stopped –play→ Playing; Playing –pause→ Paused; Playing –stop→ Stopped; Paused –play→ Playing; Paused –stop→ Stopped. Events: play, pause, stop. Test: play, pause, play, stop.
steps: Valid transitions: 5. States: 3. Table cells: 3 × 3 = 9 (5 valid + 4 invalid).
The test traverses Stopped–play, Playing–pause, Paused–play and Playing–stop: 4 distinct transitions.
Valid transition coverage = 4/5 = 80%. All states = 3/3 = 100%.
Paused–stop is missing for 100% valid transition coverage.
example.title: Solved exercise

t.sum: A state diagram shows valid states and transitions ("event [guard] / action"). The state table also shows invalid transitions (empty cells). Coverages: all states (the weakest), valid transitions or 0-switch (the most used; guarantees all states) and all transitions (valid and additionally attempts at invalid ones, one invalid per test to avoid defect masking; minimum in critical systems).

Coverage items are executable statements; coverage = executed statements / total. 100% guarantees that each statement (and therefore any defect in it) is executed at least once, but it does not detect data-dependent defects (division by zero) nor guarantee traversing all branches.

A branch is a control transfer in the flow graph, unconditional or conditional (exits from an IF, a switch, or a loop). Coverage = exercised branches / total. Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage: 100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage, but not vice versa. Nevertheless, it may not detect defects that require a specific path.

Strength: considers the entire implementation, useful even if the specification is vague or incomplete. Weakness: does not detect omission defects (requirements not implemented). It can be used in static testing (dry runs, pseudocode) and provides an objective measure of code coverage, which black-box testing alone does not offer.

Anticipates errors, defects, and failures based on how the application worked, typical developer errors, and failures in similar applications. Areas: input, output, logic, calculation, interfaces, and data. Fault attacks systematize this with a list of possible errors and tests designed to provoke them.

Design, execute, and evaluate simultaneously while learning about the product. It can be organized into sessions with a timebox, a test charter with objectives, debriefing, and session sheets. Useful with poor specifications, under time pressure, and as a complement to other techniques. It works best with experienced testers and can incorporate other techniques.

Conditions from a list based on experience, on what is important to the user, or on how the software fails are tested. Without automatable elements, without entry or exit criteria, and without overly general elements; they are usually checkable questions one by one. They must be updated according to defect analysis, without growing too large. They provide guidelines and consistency; if they are high-level, there is more variability and less repeatability.

A user story has 3 C's: Card (the medium), Conversation (how it will be used), and Confirmation (acceptance criteria). Format: "As a [role], I want [goal], so that I can [value]". It is written in collaboration from three perspectives: business, development, and testing (with brainstorming or mind maps). Good stories meet INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, and testable.

These are the conditions to accept the user story, which can be seen as test conditions; they usually come from the Conversation. They serve to define the scope, achieve consensus, describe positive and negative scenarios, serve as a basis for acceptance, and estimate. Formats: scenario-oriented (Given/When/Then, BDD) or rule-oriented (checklists or input-output tables). Other formats are accepted if they are not ambiguous.

example.problem: User Story: "As a customer, I want to withdraw cash up to my balance". Criteria: up to the balance is accepted; above is rejected with 'Insufficient funds'. Balance: 200 €.
steps: First positive case: withdraw 200 € → accepted and the balance becomes 0.
Negative case: withdraw 201 € → rejected with 'Insufficient funds' and the balance does not change.
BVA is applied within ATDD (200/201) and features are not repeated.
Finally, if applicable, a non-functional case (e.g., response time).
example.title: Solved Exercise

t.sum: Test-first approach: specification workshop (analyze the user story and its criteria, resolve ambiguities) → create tests from the criteria (by the team or by the tester), as examples. First positive cases, then negative cases, and finally non-functional cases. They must be understandable to stakeholders, cover the entire user story without going beyond it, and there cannot be two tests on the same feature. Automated, they become executable requirements.

The plan documents the means and schedule, helps meet the criteria, serves for communication, and demonstrates that the test policy and strategy are followed (or justifies deviations). Content: context (scope, objectives, test basis), assumptions and constraints, stakeholders, communication, risk register, approach (levels, types, techniques, deliverables, entry and exit criteria, independence, metrics, data, environment) and budget and schedule. More detail in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3.

Release planning (product backlog, basis for the approach and plan for all iterations): the tester helps write user stories and verifiable acceptance criteria, participates in risk analysis, estimates effort, defines the approach, and plans. Iteration planning (iteration backlog): detailed risk analysis of user stories, testability, breakdown into test tasks, estimation, and refinement of functional and non-functional aspects.

Entry criteria: preconditions to start (resources, available testware, initial quality such as passed smoke tests). Exit criteria: when to consider it finished (coverage, unresolved defects, density, failed tests, yes/no criteria). Running out of time or budget may be acceptable if stakeholders accept the risk. In agile: Definition of Ready (entry) and Definition of Done (exit).

example.problem: a = 4, m = 10, b = 22 person-days. Calculate the three-point estimate.
steps: Result: 11 ± 3 person-days, i.e., between 8 and 14.
Ratios: if development:test = 3:1 and development = 450 days → test = 450 × 1/3 = 150.
example.title: Solved exercise

t.sum: Based on metrics: by ratios (own historical data, e.g., development:test 3:2) and extrapolation (measure early in the project and extrapolate, e.g., the average of the last iterations). Based on experts: Wideband Delphi (isolated and iterative estimates until consensus; Planning Poker is a variant) and three-point: E = (a + 4m + b)/6, SD = (b − a)/6. Small tasks are estimated better: break down large ones.

example.problem: Priority (1 = highest): T1 = 2, T2 = 1 and depends on T3, T3 = 3, T4 = 4. What is the execution order?
steps: The highest priority is T2, but it depends on T3: first T3.
Then T2.
Then the next available priority: T1 (2).
Finally, T4. Order: T3, T2, T1, T4.
example.title: Solved exercise

t.sum: Strategies: risk-based (tests for the most important risks first), coverage-based (higher coverage first; additional coverage variant: each next test is the one that adds the most new coverage) and requirements-based (according to the priority of the requirements defined by stakeholders). If a high-priority test depends on a lower-priority one, the lower-priority one goes first. Resource availability also counts.

Different layers with different granularity. The higher the layer, the less granularity and isolation, and the longer the execution time. At the bottom, many small, isolated, and fast tests; at the top, few end-to-end and slow tests. Original (Cohn): unit / service / UI; another version: unit / integration / end-to-end. Helps with automation and effort distribution.

Brian Marick's model with two axes: business-oriented or technology-oriented, and supportive of the team or critical of the product. Q1 (technology, supportive): component and component integration, automated in CI. Q2 (business, supportive): functional, examples, user stories, UX prototypes, API, simulations; they check the acceptance criteria. Q3 (business, critical): exploratory, usability, UAT; often manual. Q4 (technology, critical): smoke and non-functional except usability; often automated.

A risk is a potential event or situation with an adverse effect. Probability (between 0 and 1) and impact (damage) determine the risk level: the higher, the more important its treatment. Risk management includes analysis (identification and evaluation) and control (mitigation and monitoring). Risk-based testing selects and prioritizes tests based on this analysis.

Project risks (management and control): organizational (delays, poor estimates, cuts), people (skills, conflicts, communication, lack of staff), technical (scope creep, poor tool support), and supplier risks; they affect schedule, budget, and scope. Product risks (quality characteristics): missing or incorrect functionality, incorrect calculations, runtime errors, poor architecture, response time, user experience, security. Consequences: dissatisfied users, losses, damage to third parties, sanctions, even physical damage.

Analysis = identification (brainstorming, workshops, interviews, cause-effect diagrams) + evaluation (categorize, probability, impact, level, and prioritization; quantitative like probability × impact or qualitative with a matrix). The results decide the scope, levels and types, techniques and coverage, effort, priority, and other non-testing activities. Best to start early.

Control = mitigation (applying actions to reduce the risk level) + monitoring (checking that they work, improving the evaluation, detecting new risks). Responses: mitigate with tests, accept, transfer, or contingency plan. Mitigate with tests: appropriate testers, appropriate independence, reviews and static analysis, appropriate techniques and coverage, appropriate test types, and dynamic testing, including regression.

Monitoring is collecting information about testing; controlling is issuing directives (re-prioritizing, re-evaluating criteria, adjusting the schedule, adding resources); closure consolidates experience and testware. Metrics: project progress, test progress, product quality (availability, response time, MTTF), defects (number, density, % detected), risk (residual risk), coverage, and cost.

Progress report (periodic, supports control): period, progress and deviations, impediments, metrics, new or changed risks, and plans for the next period. Completion report (at the end of a level, type, or project): summary, evaluation against the plan and exit criteria, deviations, impediments, metrics, unmitigated risks, uncorrected defects, and lessons learned. The audience determines the content, formality, and frequency.

Options: verbal, dashboards (CI/CD, boards, burn-down), electronic channels (email, chat), online documentation, and formal reports; they can be combined. Distributed teams may require more formality. Communication must be adapted to each stakeholder.

Identify, control, and track testware (plans, cases, scripts, results, logs, reports) as configuration items. An approved item becomes a baseline and only changes via change control; one can revert to a previous baseline to reproduce results. Ensures unique identification, versioning, traceability, and that testware references are unambiguous. In DevOps, this is usually automated.

t.sum: Flow from discovery to closure: record, analyze and classify, decide on the response, and close. Anomalies may not be defects (false positives, change requests). Objectives of the report: provide information for resolution, track quality, and improve processes. Content: identifier, title, date, organization and author, object and environment, context, description with steps, logs and screenshots, expected and actual results, severity, priority, status, and references.

Categories: test management (lifecycle, requirements, tests, defects, configuration), static testing (reviews and static analysis), design and implementation (generating cases, data, and procedures), execution and coverage, non-functional testing (what is difficult or impossible to do manually), DevOps (pipeline, builds, CI/CD), collaboration, scalability and standardization of deployment (virtual machines, containers), and any other that helps (even a spreadsheet).

Benefits: less repetitive manual work, consistency and repeatability (fewer human errors), more objective evaluation (coverage), more information for management, faster execution (feedback and time to market), and more time to design better tests. Risks: unrealistic expectations, poor estimates for introduction and maintenance, automating what should be done manually, over-reliance on the tool, vendor dependency, abandoned open source, incompatibility with the platform, and tools that do not comply with regulations.
